setup.flag.skill.help: Ask your agent, inside that project, what it must do before writing a line of Javadoc. If it answers from nothing, the thing you are looking for is not being picked up, and where it would have to sit for that to happen is on this page.

setup.flag.module.help: This one is the first thing read when a session starts in that folder, and it is the file this unit spends most of its words on.
setup.flag.package.label: The narrower one
setup.flag.package.help: One of these files is never read while you work at the top of the project. Go where the rules it carries actually apply.
workshop.panel.title: Flag board
workshop.panel.description: Paste each flag your graded run printed. Checked here in the browser.
workshop.panel.wrong: Not that one. Read the flag straight from the build output.
workshop.flag.coverage.label: Coverage floor
workshop.flag.coverage.hint: Ninety percent line coverage on the loans module, web and config layers excluded.
workshop.flag.coverage.help: This is a goal-shaped job, so hand it over as one, the way the goals lesson describes. Do not list the tests yourself. Give Claude the outcome and the check: get the loans module to ninety percent line coverage and keep mvn verify -Pgraded moving, without changing a public signature. To get the tests in the house style, first turn your testing convention into a skill the way the patterns lesson describes (AssertJ, one @ParameterizedTest per table of cases), then apply that skill so every test comes out the same the first time.
workshop.flag.complexity.label: Complexity ceiling
workshop.flag.complexity.hint: No method above a cyclomatic complexity of ten.
workshop.flag.complexity.help: The goals lesson calls this handing over a ceiling: no method above a cyclomatic complexity of ten. Give Claude that as the goal, not a refactor plan, and name the check it runs after each class: mvn verify -Pgraded, staying green, public signatures unchanged. The engineering lesson is the shape of the fix, extracting each decision into its own small method. If Claude keeps splitting a method the wrong way, that is a correction worth writing down: put the boundary in CLAUDE.md once, the way the patterns lesson says, so it arrives before the next attempt.
workshop.flag.honest.label: Honest coverage
workshop.flag.honest.hint: Eighty percent of mutations caught: tests that can actually fail.
workshop.flag.honest.help: This is the trap: a metric is a proxy, and Claude will satisfy the proxy. Line coverage from tests that assert nothing is green and worthless. So set the goal as the mutation score, not the coverage, and tell Claude to assert the exact fee each case returns. If it keeps writing tests that only execute the code, that is a repeating correction, and the patterns lesson says where it belongs: move it into CLAUDE.md or the testing skill, so it arrives before the mistake instead of after it.
workshop.flag.statement.label: Statement endpoint
workshop.flag.statement.hint: Implement the missing method, then read the code the endpoint returns.
workshop.flag.statement.help: This one is a plan-mode exercise, so resist typing the fix. Run mvn test -Pchallenge, then open plan mode and ask Claude to read the failing tests and plan the implementation of MemberStatements.forTier before writing anything. Check the plan against the tests yourself: it should account for filtering by tier, the loans that cost nothing, the media breakdown and the lost item, not just the first assertion. The steering lesson is why you stop it at the first gap rather than let it guess, and the engineering lesson is why the domain already hands you the fee calculation. Approve, let it implement, and stop when the tests are green. Then curl localhost:8080/api/loans/statement/STUDENT and the code is in the response.
workshop.flag.native.label: Native image
workshop.flag.native.hint: Plan a native image of step 2 that keeps its flag resource. A one-shot compiles but comes up empty.
workshop.flag.native.help: This is a plan-mode exercise like the statement flag, and a native build punishes guessing because each one costs minutes, so resist one-shotting it. In plan mode, have Claude plan a native image of step 2 using the GraalVM native-maven-plugin and the ahead-of-time step. Build it once and it comes up short: the flag lives in a classpath resource, and a native image keeps only the resources it is told to keep, so the plain build drops it and prints a miss instead of the code. That miss is the spec for the second half. Plan the resource hint it asks for, a RuntimeHintsRegistrar wired with @ImportRuntimeHints that keeps the file in the image, then build once more. This is the goals lesson's long-running outcome, so run it in a git worktree and read the diff, not the agent's word that it is done.

where.plan.label: Ask the agent to plan the same move in plan mode, read its plan against yours, and accept nothing.
audit.row.headers.remark: X-Content-Type-Options and X-Frame-Options are set, Content-Security-Policy is not. Fix: add it report-only first, then enforce it.
audit.row.audience.topic: The aud claim on a token
audit.row.audience.remark: The decoder checks the signature and the expiry and never looks at aud, so a token minted for another service in the same realm is accepted. Fix: add an audience validator.
audit.row.errors.remark: The handler puts the exception message in the body. On a constraint violation that prints the column names with it. Fix: log it, return a code.

flow-naive.description: You talk to the agent, the agent writes the code inside the project. Nothing comes back either way.
flow-plan.description: You and the agent talk both ways, then the agent writes the code inside the project.
flow-spec.description: You and the agent talk both ways, and so do the agent and the project, which holds the spec the code is built from.
flow-audit.description: You ask the agent, the agent writes audit.md, you read it, you hand rows back to the agent, and the agent changes the project, which holds the code and a spec it does not have to have. Underneath, the changed project comes back to you and you take it up into audit.md, which is updated from the project above.

agents-at-once.description: Four arrangements drawn as wires from you to the agents you are running. One agent on a single solid teal wire. Then four agents on four thin muted ones, none of them teal. Then one teal wire to an agent that holds the wires to the same four itself. Then one teal wire to an agent in front, with three dashed wires to agents running behind it.

two-windows.description: Two context windows side by side. In the left one the wrong file sits in the window in full, with your correction under it and the next turn after that, and all of it is re-sent on every turn. In the right one the request is rewritten, the turns after it are gone, and the window holds only the better request and the work.

quiz.small-change-no-spec.question: Your team keeps one spec file per feature and you follow it. Today's list is a log line in the wrong place and a column that should have been nullable. Writing the specs would take longer than the changes do. What is the right call?
quiz.small-change-no-spec.nudge: Make them naive, straight into the code. Nudging is not restructuring, and a change that decides nothing does not earn a workflow.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.consistency: Write the specs anyway. A workflow you apply only when you feel like it stops being a workflow, and the exceptions are where the drift starts.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.batch: Hold the small changes back until there are enough of them to cover in one spec, so the file count stays sensible.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.audit: Make the changes, then run an audit over the repository, which is the pass that catches whatever the small ones broke.
quiz.small-change-no-spec.explanation: A spec is worth writing when something is being decided. A log line and a nullable column decide nothing, so the spec is cost with no answer in it.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.question: You stop asking for changes and start asking for a plan first, every time. The work that comes back is better, which surprises you, because you approve most of the plans with barely an edit. Where did the gain come from?
quiz.plan-mode-interview.interview: The plan interviewed you. Its questions were the decisions you had skipped, and you answered them before a line of code existed.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.thinking: The model reasons for longer before it writes, and that extra thinking comes back to you as a better first draft.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.document: The plan stays in the repository beside the code, so the next session starts from what this one decided.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.review: Reading a plan is faster than reading a diff, so you catch the mistakes earlier and it costs you less to say no.
quiz.plan-mode-interview.explanation: You approve most plans because answering the questions was the work. The agent asks which tier gets a grace period and what happens when the list comes back empty, and the workflow puts you back in the design.
quiz.audit-as-essay.question: You ask an agent whether a module is complete, secure and consistent with the rest of the repository. Back come four pages of prose. You read it once, agree with most of it, and a week later you cannot remember which parts you dealt with. What went wrong?
quiz.audit-as-essay.format: You did not ask for a format. A table holds it down to what you can act on, and it lives in the repository, so next week it still says which row you were on.
quiz.audit-as-essay.scope: You asked about three things at once. Run completeness, security and style as separate passes and each answer comes back short enough to act on.
quiz.audit-as-essay.memory: The session ended and the reading went with it. Paste the report back in at the start of the next one and carry on from where it stopped.
quiz.audit-as-essay.model: Prose is what a model falls back on when it is not confident. A narrower question would have got you a narrower answer.
quiz.audit-as-essay.explanation: An audit is a file in your repository, so it diffs and gets reviewed the way the code does. Ask for the topic, where it lives, how solid it is and what to do about it, and you have rows to work rather than paragraphs to re-read.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.question: You hand over a module nobody has touched in years with one line: make this code cleaner and keep the tests green. Four hours and a small fortune in tokens later it reports that the work is done. The diff is enormous and the code looks about the same. What went wrong?
quiz.report-on-a-wish.no-command: Nothing could say no. There was no command that answers yes or no, so the run had nothing to fail against and stopped when it felt finished.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.too-long: The run was too long to hold together. Broken into four one-hour goals it would have kept its bearings and each piece would have landed.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.wrong-tier: The tier was wrong for the job. Refactoring is judgement work, and a cheaper model spends a long run rewriting rather than deciding.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.no-worktree: It ran on your branch. Working next to your own edits, it kept rereading files that were changing under it and lost track of what it had done.
quiz.report-on-a-wish.explanation: A goal is a task with an outcome something else can measure, and "cleaner" is not one. Name the command that prints the answer, a coverage floor or a complexity ceiling, and the run has something to run until.
quiz.fleet-bill.question: You have five specs written, so you fan them out across five agents instead of working through them yourself. Everything lands inside the hour, which is what you wanted. The token bill is several times what those five jobs cost you last month, one after another, in one session. Where did it go?
quiz.fleet-bill.read-again: Every agent started on an empty context, so every one of them read its way into the project again before it wrote anything.
quiz.fleet-bill.overwrote: The agents worked the same files at the same time, so a good part of the run was work being written over and done a second time.
quiz.fleet-bill.gathered: Everything the agents produced was gathered back into one window at the end, and that transcript is re-sent on every turn after it.
quiz.fleet-bill.pricier-tier: A fan-out runs on the top tier by default, because coordinating several agents is the kind of work the cheaper tiers cannot hold together.
quiz.fleet-bill.explanation: The same CLAUDE.md, the same files and the same working out are paid for once per agent, and none of them learn anything from the others. That is the trade: you buy wall-clock time with tokens.
quiz.window-tail.question: You are on a subscription that meters you in a rolling five-hour window. Everything you cared about today is finished and reviewed, and there are thirty-five minutes of window left. What is the best use of them?
quiz.window-tail.spend-it: Start something expensive you wanted anyway. A design pass or a fleet against specs you already wrote, so the tail goes on real work instead of expiring.
quiz.window-tail.save-it: Leave it. What you do not spend rolls into the next window, so a quiet afternoon is what buys you a heavy morning tomorrow.
quiz.window-tail.stop-early: Stop working and let the window turn over early, so the next one starts clean instead of half spent when you need it.
quiz.window-tail.upgrade-small: Put the small jobs left on your list on the frontier model. The window is paid for either way, so the highest tier is the one to spend it at.
quiz.window-tail.explanation: Unspent window is not carried anywhere, so the tail of one is the cheapest moment for a move you were going to make sooner or later. Spending it at a higher tier on work that never needed one buys nothing.
